text:
Research supports ranking-aware audits, but does not establish history-intervention sensitivity as a predictor of ranking improvement. [Beyond Top-1](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2026/926) finds top-1 counterfactual evaluation inconsistent and recommends top-k assessment. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) shows sampled evaluation can reverse model comparisons. For this benchmark, retain the pinned sampled HR@10 objective; interpret full-catalog intervention results as diagnostics, without assuming equivalent model rankings.

A reproducible protocol would freeze users, checkpoints, histories, category catalogs, eligibility masks, seeds and tie-breaking. Exclude every item in the original observed history throughout interventions, preventing deleted items from becoming newly eligible. Define overlap@k = |T_original ∩ T_intervened|/k; signed rank displacement = rank_intervened(i) − rank_original(i), positive meaning demotion, evaluated for fixed original top-k items over the same eligible catalog. Report mean absolute displacement separately. Repeat targeted deletions against random deletions matched on count and history-position strata; use matched shuffle controls for order interventions. Measure both deterministic rerun agreement and variation across intervention seeds. These are proposed operational definitions, rather than a single established standard.

Assess predictive value prospectively: record diagnostic signals before observing each subsequent trial’s validation gain, then estimate their association with paired HR@10 improvements across trials. Compare diagnostic-guided proposals with matched-budget unguided proposals; report category-stratified paired user-bootstrap intervals, preserving equal category weights, plus variation across trials. [Offline evaluation options](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-020-09371-3) supports explicit protocols and paired statistical comparisons. Bound cost with fixed users/category, intervention counts and checkpoints; cache baseline scores and batch catalog scoring. Keep the simulator’s twenty users separate from stronger population-level claims. Charge all audit computation to the search budget; leave hidden tests untouched.
